1:1.t: Jeremiah prophesied from 627 BC, the thirteenth year of King Josiah, until after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Anathoth was a town of priests about five kilometers northeast of Jerusalem.

1:6.t: "Too young": the KJV's "a child"; Hebrew na'ar, a youth.

1:11.t: A wordplay in Hebrew: the almond tree (shaqed, "the watchful tree", the first to blossom in spring) and "watching" (shoqed).

2:10.t: "Cyprus": the KJV's "the isles of Chittim", the far west. Kedar is in the eastern desert.

2:16.t: Memphis (the KJV's "Noph") and Tahpanhes were cities of Egypt.

2:18.t: "The Nile ... the Euphrates": the KJV's "Sihor ... the river".

2:25.t: "Do not run until your feet are bare": the KJV reads "Withhold thy foot from being unshod".

2:34.t: "Though you did not catch them breaking in": breaking in was the one case where killing a thief was not murder (Exodus 22:2).

3:1.t: Deuteronomy 24:1-4 forbade a man to remarry a wife he had divorced after she married another. Yet God invites unfaithful Israel to return.

3:6.t: "Faithless Israel ... unfaithful Judah": the northern kingdom had already fallen to Assyria (722 BC). Judah saw it and did not learn.

3:22.t: "I will cure you of backsliding": a wordplay in Hebrew, shuvu banim shovavim ("return, backsliding children").

3:24.t: "Shameful gods": the KJV's "shame", a mocking name for Baal (Hebrew boshet).

4:15.t: Dan and the hills of Ephraim lay to the north, the direction from which the invader came.

4:30.t: "Highlight your eyes with makeup": the KJV's "rentest thy face with painting".

5:10.t: "Vineyards": the KJV's "walls"; the Hebrew shuroteha may mean either "her rows (of vines)" or "her walls".

5:24.t: "Autumn and spring rains": the KJV's "the former and the latter".

5:31.t: "By their own authority": the KJV's "by their means", literally "at their hands".

6:1.t: Tekoa and Beth Hakkerem were towns south of Jerusalem.

6:2.t: "I will destroy Daughter Zion": the KJV reads "I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman". The Hebrew damiti can mean either.

6:27.t: "A tester of metals": the KJV's "a tower and a fortress". The Hebrew bachon means an assayer. Verses 28-30 describe a failed refining.

7:12.t: Shiloh: the place where the tabernacle stood in the days of Eli; it was destroyed, probably by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4, Psalm 78:60).

7:18.t: "The Queen of Heaven": probably the goddess Ishtar or Asherah, worshiped with cakes and drink offerings. See 44:17-19.

7:22.t: "I did not just give them commands about burnt offerings": the KJV reads "I spake not ... concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices". The point is that sacrifice without obedience was never what God wanted (1 Samuel 15:22).

7:31.t: Topheth and the Valley of Ben Hinnom: Topheth was the place in the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned as sacrifices (see Isaiah 30:33). The Hebrew name of the valley, Ge-Hinnom, became Gehenna, the New Testament word for hell.

8:7.t: "The dove, the swift and the thrush": the KJV's "the turtle and the crane and the swallow"; the birds are uncertain.

8:8.t: "The lying pen of the scribes has handled it falsely": the KJV's "Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain."

8:18.t: "You who are my Comforter in sorrow": the KJV's "When I would comfort myself against sorrow". The Hebrew is uncertain.

8:22.t: Gilead, east of the Jordan, was known for its healing balm (Genesis 37:25).

9:1.t: In the Hebrew this verse is 8:23, and 9:1-26 is 9:2-26.

9:15.t: "Bitter food and ... poisoned water": the KJV's "wormwood ... water of gall".

10:5.t: "Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field": the KJV's "upright as the palm tree". The Hebrew tomer may mean a palm tree or a scarecrow.

10:9.t: Uphaz: an unknown place, perhaps Ophir.

10:11.t: This verse is written in Aramaic, the international language of the time, as a message the exiles could give to their captors.

11:5.t: "Amen": the KJV's "So be it", the response of agreement to the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 27:15-26).

11:13.t: "That shameful god Baal": the KJV's "that shameful thing"; the Hebrew boshet, "shame", is a mocking name for Baal (see 3:24).

11:15.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

11:20.t: "Heart and mind": the KJV's "the reins and the heart", literally "kidneys and heart".

11:21.t: Jeremiah's own townspeople at Anathoth plotted to kill him.

12:5.t: "The thickets by the Jordan": the KJV's "the swelling of Jordan", the dense jungle along the river where lions lived.

13:1.t: "Belt": the KJV's "girdle", a linen undergarment worn around the waist.

13:4.t: "The Euphrates": the Hebrew perat may be the Euphrates or Parah, a place near Anathoth.

13:12.t: "Wineskin": the KJV's "bottle"; the Hebrew nevel can also mean a clay jar.

13:18.t: "The queen mother": probably Nehushta, mother of King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:8-15).

13:23.t: "Ethiopian": Hebrew kushi, a person from Cush.
"Can a leopard change its spots?": sin had become second nature. Only God can change the heart (31:33, Ezekiel 36:26).

15:1.t: Moses and Samuel were famous for interceding for Israel (Exodus 32:11-14, 1 Samuel 7:9, 12:23).

15:4.t: Manasseh's idolatry and bloodshed sealed Judah's judgment (2 Kings 21:1-16, 23:26).

15:11.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

15:12.t: "Iron from the north": Babylon's power cannot be broken.

16:2.t: Jeremiah's unmarried life was itself a sign of coming disaster.

16:6.t: Cutting oneself and shaving the head were mourning customs forbidden in Israel (Deuteronomy 14:1).

16:21.t: The KJV margin notes that "The LORD" here translates the name JEHOVAH (YHWH).

17:1.t: "Flint point": the KJV's "the point of a diamond".

17:6.t: "A bush in the wastelands": the KJV's "the heath in the desert", probably a juniper.

17:11.t: Partridges were thought to hatch eggs they had not laid.

17:13.t: "Written in the dust": their names will vanish like writing in the dirt.

17:16.t: "Run away from being Your shepherd": the KJV's "hastened from being a pastor to follow thee".

17:19.t: "The People's Gate": the KJV's "the gate of the children of the people".

17:26.t: "The western foothills ... the Negev": the KJV's "the plain ... the south".

18:14.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

19:1.t: "Clay jar": the KJV's "earthen bottle", a narrow-necked water jug.

19:2.t: "The Potsherd Gate": the KJV's "the east gate"; the Hebrew charsit means "potsherds".

19:9.t: Fulfilled in the siege of Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:10).

20:1.t: "Pashhur": the KJV's "Pashur", a different man from the Pashhur of 21:1.

21:2.t: "Nebuchadnezzar": the KJV's "Nebuchadrezzar", a closer form of the Babylonian name Nabu-kudurri-usur. Jeremiah usually uses this spelling; the familiar form is used here throughout.

21:13.t: "You who live above this valley on the rocky plateau": the KJV's "O inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain".

22:10.t: The "dead king" is Josiah, killed in battle in 609 BC. The exile is his son Shallum (Jehoahaz), taken to Egypt (2 Kings 23:29-34).

22:20.t: "Abarim": the KJV's "the passages", the mountain range in Moab.

22:24.t: "Jehoiachin": the KJV's "Coniah", a short form of his name.

22:30.t: Jehoiachin did have sons (1 Chronicles 3:17), but none of them reigned. "As if childless" means as far as the throne was concerned.

23:6.t: "The LORD Our Righteousness": the KJV prints THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS; Hebrew YHWH tsidqenu. The name is a wordplay on Zedekiah ("the LORD is righteous"), the faithless last king of Judah. The same name is given to Jerusalem in 33:16.

23:10.t: "Because of the curse": the KJV's "because of swearing"; the Hebrew alah can mean either.

23:15.t: "Bitter food ... poisoned water": the KJV's "wormwood ... the water of gall".

23:33.t: A wordplay on massa, which means both "burden" and "prophetic message". The people mockingly asked for "the burden from the LORD"; God answers that they themselves are the burden.

24:1.t: "Jehoiachin": the KJV's "Jeconiah". The exile of 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10-16).

25:1.t: The fourth year of Jehoiakim was 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish.

25:9.t: "My servant Nebuchadnezzar": the pagan king is God's instrument of judgment, as Assyria was in Isaiah 10:5.

25:26.t: "Sheshak": a code name for Babylon (51:41), formed by a Hebrew letter-substitution cipher.

25:38.t: "The sword of the oppressor": the KJV's "the fierceness of the oppressor"; many Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek read "sword".

26:1.t: This chapter tells what happened after the temple sermon of chapter 7, in 609-608 BC.

26:19.t: The KJV's source text adds a marginal note to this verse ("Heb. the face of the LORD"), not part of the verse.

26:24.t: Ahikam was the father of Gedaliah, later governor of Judah (40:5).

27:1.t: "Jehoiakim": following the KJV and the standard Hebrew. Verses 3, 12 and 20 and 28:1 show that these events took place under Zedekiah, and a few Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read "Zedekiah".

27:19.t: "The bronze Sea, the movable stands": the great basin and the wheeled carts made by Solomon (1 Kings 7:23-37).

28:1.t: "The fourth year" of Zedekiah was 594-593 BC.

30:6.t: "On his stomach": the KJV's "on his loins".

30:9.t: "David their king": the coming King from David's line (23:5, Ezekiel 34:23-24, Hosea 3:5).

31:3.t: "Appeared to us": the KJV's "hath appeared of old unto me". The Greek reads "to him".

"Everlasting love ... steadfast love" (Hebrew ahavat olam ... hesed): God's love that never ends, the KJV's "everlasting love ... lovingkindness". "Drawn you": led you out with kindness, as one draws a loved one close (Hosea 11:4).

31:15.t: Ramah, north of Jerusalem, was near Rachel's tomb and was where exiles were gathered for deportation (40:1). Matthew 2:18 quotes this verse of the mothers of Bethlehem.

31:22.t: "The woman will surround the man": the KJV's "A woman shall compass a man". The meaning is uncertain; it may mean that Israel, the unfaithful bride, will return to embrace her husband, the LORD.

31:23.t: "You prosperous city": the KJV's "O habitation of justice"; the Hebrew neveh tsedeq means "abode of righteousness".

32:1.t: The tenth year of Zedekiah was 587 BC, during the final siege of Jerusalem.

32:7.t: "As nearest relative it is your right and duty to buy it": the KJV's "the right of redemption is thine". The go'el, the kinsman-redeemer, bought back family land so that it stayed in the family. See Leviticus 25:25.

32:9.t: "About two hundred grams of silver": the KJV's "seventeen shekels of silver".

32:11.t: Deeds were written twice on one document; one copy was rolled up and sealed, the other left open for reference.

33:2.t: "He who made the earth": the KJV's "the maker thereof"; the Greek reads "who made the earth". The KJV margin notes that "the LORD" here is JEHOVAH.

33:13.t: "The one who counts them": a shepherd counted his sheep as they passed under his staff (Leviticus 27:32).

33:16.t: "The LORD Our Righteousness" (Hebrew YHWH tsidqenu): the name given to the coming King at 23:6, a wordplay on Zedekiah ("the LORD is righteous"); here the name is given to Jerusalem, the city that reflects her King.

34:5.t: "A funeral fire": the KJV's "the burnings of thy fathers", the burning of spices in honor of a dead king (2 Chronicles 16:14).

34:7.t: Lachish and Azekah were fortresses southwest of Jerusalem. A letter found at Lachish from this time says that the signals of Azekah could no longer be seen.

34:18.t: Walking between the halves of a slaughtered animal sealed a covenant: "may I be cut in two like this if I break it" (Genesis 15:9-17).

35:2.t: The Rechabites were a clan descended from Jonadab son of Rechab, a zealous supporter of Jehu (2 Kings 10:15-23). They kept a nomadic way of life.

36:1.t: The fourth year of Jehoiakim was 605 BC.

36:23.t: "Columns": the KJV's "leaves". "A scribe's knife": the KJV's "penknife", used to trim reed pens.

Jehoiakim's burning of the scroll contrasts with his father Josiah, who tore his clothes in repentance when the book of the law was read to him (2 Kings 22:11). God's word cannot be destroyed (verse 32; Isaiah 40:8).

36:26.t: "A son of the king": the KJV's "the son of Hammelech"; hammelech means "the king".

37:12.t: "To get his share of the property": the KJV's "to separate himself thence in the midst of the people". Compare 32:6-15.

38:6.t: "Cistern": the KJV's "dungeon", a pit for storing rainwater.

Jeremiah was rescued by Ebed-melech, a foreigner and a palace servant, when the leaders of his own people left him to die. In 39:18 God rewards his faith: "because you trust in Me" (Hebrew ki vatachta bi).

38:7.t: "Cushite": the KJV's "Ethiopian". Ebed-melech means "servant of the king".

38:28.t: The last sentence leads into chapter 39. The KJV reads "and he was there when Jerusalem was taken".

39:1.t: Compare 2 Kings 25:1-12 and Jeremiah 52:4-16. The siege began in January 588 BC; the wall was breached in July 586 BC.

39:3.t: "Nergal-sharezer of Samgar, Nebo-sarsekim, a chief officer, Nergal-sharezer, a high official": the KJV's "Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebo, Sarsechim, Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer, Rab-mag". Rab-saris and Rab-mag are Babylonian titles. A clay tablet naming Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, a chief officer of Nebuchadnezzar, matches Nebo-sarsekim.

39:4.t: "The Arabah": the KJV's "the plain", the Jordan Valley.

40:6.t: Mizpah, a town about thirteen kilometers north of Jerusalem, became the center of government after Jerusalem fell.

41:1.t: The seventh month was probably about two months after the fall of Jerusalem. The Jewish fast of Gedaliah still remembers his murder.

41:5.t: The pilgrims mourned the destroyed temple, but still brought offerings to its site.

41:12.t: "The great pool in Gibeon": the KJV's "the great waters that are in Gibeon". See 2 Samuel 2:13.

41:17.t: "Geruth Kimham": the KJV's "the habitation of Chimham". Kimham was a friend of David (2 Samuel 19:37-40).

42:20.t: "You made a fatal mistake": the KJV's "ye dissembled in your hearts".

43:7.t: Tahpanhes was a fortress city in the eastern Nile delta.

43:9.t: "Brick pavement": the KJV's "the clay in the brickkiln".

43:12.t: "As a shepherd picks his garment clean of lice": the KJV's "he shall array himself with the land of Egypt, as a shepherd putteth on his garment". The Hebrew ataf can mean either "wrap" or "delouse".

43:13.t: "The temple of the sun": the KJV's "Beth-shemesh", the Hebrew name for Heliopolis ("city of the sun") in Egypt. "Sacred pillars": the KJV's "images", obelisks.

44:1.t: "Lower Egypt ... Memphis ... Upper Egypt": the KJV's "Egypt ... Noph ... the country of Pathros".

44:17.t: "The Queen of Heaven": probably the goddess Ishtar or Asherah, worshiped with cakes and drink offerings; see 7:18.

44:19.t: "Did not our husbands know": vows by married women needed their husbands' consent (Numbers 30:6-15).

44:30.t: Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) was killed in 570 BC.

45:1.t: This message to Baruch dates from 605 BC (compare 36:1), earlier than the surrounding chapters.

46:2.t: The battle of Carchemish in 605 BC ended Egypt's power in Syria and Canaan.

46:9.t: Cush, Put and Lydia: regions south and west of Egypt that supplied soldiers.

46:18.t: Tabor and Carmel stand out above the surrounding land; so Nebuchadnezzar will tower over Egypt.

46:25.t: "Amon god of Thebes": the KJV's "the multitude of No"; Hebrew amon minno, Amon of No (Thebes).

47:4.t: Caphtor: Crete, the Philistines' place of origin (Amos 9:7).

47:5.t: "Will be silenced": the KJV's "is cut off". "You remnant on the plain": the KJV's "the remnant of their valley".

48:1.t: "The stronghold": the KJV's "Misgab", which means "high fortress".

48:2.t: "Madmen": a town in Moab, a wordplay on dmm, "be silent".

48:6.t: "A bush in the desert": the KJV's "the heath in the wilderness".

48:7.t: Chemosh was the national god of Moab (Numbers 21:29).

48:9.t: "Put salt on Moab": the KJV's "Give wings unto Moab". The Hebrew tsits is uncertain.

48:11.t: Wine left too long on its dregs grows thick and stale. Moab had never been "poured out" by exile, so it had grown complacent. Compare Zephaniah 1:12, which uses the same picture.

49:1.t: "Molech": the KJV's "their king"; the Hebrew malkam can be read as Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5).

49:3.t: "Molech": the KJV's "their king"; the Hebrew malkam can be read as Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5).

49:4.t: "Valleys so fruitful": the KJV's "thy flowing valley".

49:8.t: Dedan was a trading people south of Edom.

49:19.t: "The thickets of the Jordan": the KJV's "the swelling of Jordan", the dense jungle along the river where lions lived; see 12:5.

50:44.t: "The thickets of the Jordan": the KJV's "the swelling of Jordan", the dense jungle along the river where lions lived; see 12:5.

49:20.t: "Their pasture will be appalled at their fate": the KJV's "surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them".

50:45.t: "Their pasture will be appalled at their fate": the KJV's "surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them".

49:21.t: "The Red Sea": the Hebrew yam suph, "Sea of Reeds".

49:28.t: Kedar and Hazor: Arabian tribes and settlements of the eastern desert.

49:34.t: Elam lay east of Babylon, in what is now southwestern Iran.

50:2.t: "Marduk": the KJV's "Merodach", the chief god of Babylon. Bel ("lord") was his title.

50:7.t: "Their true pasture": the KJV's "the habitation of justice".

50:11.t: "Threshing grain": the KJV's "at grass"; the Hebrew dashah may be read either way.

50:21.t: Merathaim ("double rebellion") and Pekod ("punishment") are wordplays on names of regions in Babylonia.

50:36.t: "Her false prophets": the KJV's "the liars"; the Hebrew baddim means "empty talkers".

50:41.t: These verses repeat 6:22-24, now turned against Babylon.

51:1.t: "Leb Kamai": the KJV's "them that dwell in the midst of them that rise up against me". Leb Kamai is a code name for Chaldea, formed by the same letter-substitution cipher as Sheshak (25:26).

51:3.t: "Let not the archer string his bow": the KJV's "Against him that bendeth let the archer bend his bow". The Hebrew is uncertain.

51:27.t: Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz: peoples of the mountains north of Babylon, later subject to the Medes.

51:39.t: "Shout with laughter": Babylon fell during a feast (Daniel 5).

51:59.t: "The staff officer": the KJV's "a quiet prince"; the Hebrew sar menuchah may mean "quartermaster", the officer responsible for resting places on a journey. Seraiah was probably Baruch's brother (32:12).

51:64.t: "And her people will fall": the KJV's "and they shall be weary", repeating the last words of verse 58.

52:21.t: "About 8.1 meters high and about 5.4 meters around; each was about 8 centimeters thick": the KJV's "eighteen cubits ... a fillet of twelve cubits ... four fingers".

52:22.t: "About 2.3 meters": the KJV's "five cubits". 2 Kings 25:17 reads three cubits.

52:28.t: These smaller numbers are probably men only, or only certain groups. The seventh year is 597 BC; the eighteenth is 586 BC; the twenty-third is 582 BC.

52:31.t: Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) became king in 562 BC. "Twenty-fifth day": 2 Kings 25:27 reads the twenty-seventh.
The book ends with the release of Jehoiachin, the king from David's line. Even in exile, God's promise to David has not failed (2 Samuel 7:16, Jeremiah 33:17).

1:5.t: "I knew you ... I set you apart" (Hebrew yeda'tikha ... hiqdashtikha): "knew" means chose in a personal relationship (as in Amos 3:2); "set apart" means consecrated, made holy for God's purpose. God's call on Jeremiah came before his birth. Compare Galatians 1:15.

2:2.t: "The devotion of your youth" (Hebrew hesed ne'urayikh): Israel's hesed toward God, her loyal love as a young bride, the KJV's "the kindness of thy youth".

2:13.t: "The spring of living water" (Hebrew meqor mayim chayyim): flowing, fresh water, in contrast to stale water stored in a cracked cistern. Jesus offers "living water" (John 4:10-14, 7:37-38).

3:12.t: "I am faithful" (Hebrew chasid ani): the KJV's "I am merciful", from hesed: "I am one who shows steadfast love".

3:14.t: "I am your husband" (Hebrew anokhi ba'alti bakhem): the verb ba'al, "to be master or husband", is a pointed wordplay on Baal, the god Israel had chased.

3:16.t: "The ark of the covenant": in the coming age the ark will not be needed, for all Jerusalem will be God's throne.

4:4.t: "Circumcise your hearts": outward circumcision was to be matched by an inward one, a heart opened to God; outward signs mean nothing without an inward change. See Deuteronomy 10:16, 30:6 and Romans 2:29.

4:23.t: "Formless and empty" (Hebrew tohu vavohu): the words of Genesis 1:2. Judgment is pictured as creation running backward into chaos.

6:14.t: "Peace, peace ... when there is no peace" (Hebrew shalom shalom ve'en shalom): the false prophets promised well-being while ignoring the people's sickness of sin. The words are repeated in 8:11.

6:16.t: "You will find rest for your souls": Jesus echoes these words in Matthew 11:29.

7:4.t: "The temple of the LORD" repeated three times: the people treated the temple like a lucky charm, as if God's house guaranteed their safety whatever they did.

7:11.t: "A den of robbers": a hideout where thieves feel safe between crimes. Jesus quotes these words when He drives out the money changers (Matthew 21:13).

9:23.t: "Let the one who boasts boast about this ... to know Me": Paul quotes this in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17. "Steadfast love, justice and righteousness" (Hebrew hesed, mishpat, utsedaqah): the qualities God delights in and wants in His people. The KJV's "lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness".

10:10.t: "The true God ... the living God" (Hebrew YHWH elohim emet ... elohim chayyim): emet means truth and faithfulness; the LORD is real and reliable, unlike the lifeless idols.

10:23.t: "People's lives are not their own": the KJV's "the way of man is not in himself". Compare Proverbs 16:9 and 20:24.

12:1.t: "Why does the way of the wicked prosper?": one of Jeremiah's "confessions", honest complaints to God (also 11:18-23, 15:10-21, 17:14-18, 18:19-23, 20:7-18). Compare Job 21 and Psalm 73.

13:11.t: "As a belt is bound around the waist" (Hebrew yidbaq): the verb davaq, "to cling", as in Genesis 2:24. God made Israel cling to Him as closely as a garment; separated from Him, they became useless.

15:16.t: "When Your words came, I ate them": Jeremiah took God's word into himself; see Ezekiel 3:1-3 and Revelation 10:9-10.

15:19.t: "If you repent, I will restore you" (Hebrew im tashuv va'ashivkha): a wordplay on shuv, "return". Even the prophet must turn back to God before speaking for Him. "My spokesman": literally "like My mouth".

16:5.t: "My peace, My steadfast love and My compassion" (Hebrew shalom, hesed, rachamim): the three blessings God withdraws in judgment.

16:14.t: "As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north": the return from exile will be a new exodus, greater than the first. Repeated in 23:7-8.

17:5.t: Cursed and blessed: a contrast like Psalm 1. "Trusts" (Hebrew batach): to rely on, feel secure in. A tree by the water draws life from a source deeper than the weather.

17:9.t: "Deceitful ... beyond cure" (Hebrew aqov ... anush): the heart is crooked and incurably sick; the KJV's "desperately wicked". Only God can search it (verse 10) and make it new (31:33).

18:6.t: "Like clay in the hand of the potter": God is free to reshape a nation that repents or rebels (verses 7-10). Paul draws on this picture in Romans 9:20-21.

20:7.t: "You deceived me ... You overpowered me" (Hebrew pittitani ... chazaqtani): the verb patah means to persuade, entice or seduce. Jeremiah felt that God had drawn him into a calling he could not escape.

20:9.t: "Like a fire shut up in my bones": the prophet could not stop speaking God's word even when it brought him suffering. Compare 1 Corinthians 9:16.

22:16.t: "Is that not what it means to know Me?": to know God (Hebrew da'at) is not only to have knowledge about Him, but to share His concern for the poor and needy. Compare 9:24 and 1 John 3:17-18.

23:5.t: "A righteous Branch" (Hebrew tsemach tsaddiq): a descendant of David who will reign as the true King. See Isaiah 4:2, 11:1, Jeremiah 33:15 and Zechariah 3:8. Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus, through whom God's people receive righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30). Following this reading, the King's pronouns are capitalized.

23:18.t: "The council of the LORD" (Hebrew sod YHWH): the heavenly assembly where God's purposes are made known. True prophets are those who have stood there (1 Kings 22:19-23, Amos 3:7).

23:22.t: "The council of the LORD" (Hebrew sod YHWH): the heavenly assembly where God's purposes are made known. True prophets are those who have stood there (1 Kings 22:19-23, Amos 3:7).

23:24.t: "Do not I fill heaven and earth?": God is present everywhere; no one can hide from Him. Compare Psalm 139:7-12.

24:7.t: "I will give them a heart to know Me": a promise developed in the new covenant (31:33-34).

25:11.t: "Seventy years": the length of Babylon's rule, from about 609 to 539 BC, or the temple's ruin from 586 to its rebuilding in 516 BC. Daniel studied this prophecy (Daniel 9:2), and 2 Chronicles 36:21 sees it fulfilled.

25:15.t: "The cup ... of the wine of My wrath": a picture of judgment drunk to the dregs. Jesus speaks of the cup He must drink (Mark 14:36); see also Revelation 14:10.

26:3.t: "Then I will relent" (Hebrew venichamti): God's warnings were meant to bring repentance. See 18:7-8.

29:7.t: "Seek the peace and prosperity of the city" (Hebrew shalom ha'ir): the exiles were to work and pray for the good of Babylon, the city of their captors. Compare 1 Timothy 2:1-2.

29:11.t: "Plans for peace and not for disaster, to give you a future and a hope" (Hebrew machshevot shalom ... acharit vetiqvah): the KJV's "thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end". Spoken to exiles facing seventy years in Babylon, the promise was that God's purpose for His people would not fail, even when they would not live to see it.

29:13.t: "When you seek Me with all your heart": the heart in Hebrew is the center of thought and will, so this means with your whole being; see Deuteronomy 4:29.

30:7.t: "A time of trouble for Jacob" (Hebrew et tsarah leya'aqov): a time of distress without equal, from which God's people will be rescued.

31:20.t: "My heart yearns for him" (Hebrew hamu me'ai): literally "My inner parts are stirred", the KJV's "my bowels are troubled". God's love for wayward Ephraim is like a parent's anguish. "Compassion" (rachem): from rechem, "womb", a mother's tender love; see Exodus 34:6.

31:31.t: "A new covenant" (Hebrew berit chadashah): the only place in the Old Testament that uses this phrase. Unlike the covenant at Sinai, written on stone and broken, this one is written on the heart, brings personal knowledge of God, and is based on complete forgiveness. Jesus spoke of "the new covenant in My blood" at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews 8:8-12 and 10:16-17 quote this passage at length.

31:33.t: "In their minds" (Hebrew beqirbam): literally "in their inward parts", the KJV's "inward parts". God's instruction will be part of who they are, not only an outward rule. Compare Ezekiel 36:26-27 and 2 Corinthians 3:3.

32:17.t: "Nothing is too hard for You ... Is anything too hard for Me?" (Hebrew lo yippale): the same question God asked Abraham about Sarah's son (Genesis 18:14). Buying land in a city about to fall was an act of faith that God would bring His people back.

32:27.t: "Nothing is too hard for You ... Is anything too hard for Me?" (Hebrew lo yippale): the same question God asked Abraham about Sarah's son (Genesis 18:14). Buying land in a city about to fall was an act of faith that God would bring His people back.

32:40.t: "An everlasting covenant" (Hebrew berit olam): the new covenant of 31:31-34, written on the heart and based on complete forgiveness.

33:3.t: "Unsearchable things" (Hebrew betsurot): literally "fortified" or "inaccessible" things, hidden from human understanding until God reveals them.

33:15.t: "A righteous Branch" (Hebrew tsemach tsaddiq): a descendant of David who will reign as the true King; Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus. See 23:5.

34:17.t: "I now proclaim freedom for you" (Hebrew deror): a bitter wordplay. The people took back the freedom (deror) they had proclaimed to their slaves, so God "frees" them to the sword. Deror is the word for the Jubilee release (Leviticus 25:10).

35:14.t: The Rechabites' faithfulness to a human ancestor's command shames Judah's unfaithfulness to the living God.

42:6.t: "Whether it is favorable or unfavorable, we will obey": the people promised obedience, but had already made up their minds. True seeking of God's will means being willing to hear "no".

45:5.t: "Should you then seek great things for yourself?": when God is overturning a whole world, Baruch's ambitions must give way. His reward is his life, preserved as a prize of war (the KJV's "for a prey").

48:47.t: "Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab": even in judgment on enemy nations, God leaves room for mercy (also 46:26, 49:6, 49:39). Ruth, the Moabite, became an ancestor of David and of Jesus.

50:20.t: "Search will be made for Israel's guilt, but there will be none": a picture of complete forgiveness under the new covenant (31:34).

50:34.t: "Their Redeemer is strong" (Hebrew go'alam chazaq): the go'el was the kinsman who rescued a family member. God is the kinsman who will defend His people's cause in court and set them free. See Isaiah 41:14.

51:6.t: "Flee from Babylon! ... Come out of her, My people!": Revelation 18:4 echoes these verses about the final Babylon.

51:45.t: "Flee from Babylon! ... Come out of her, My people!": Revelation 18:4 echoes these verses about the final Babylon.
